tip: Adjectives in '-lig' add '-en' to form adverbs: 'daglig' (daily) becomes 'dagligen'.
Language names are lowercase in Swedish: 'engelska', not 'Engelska'.
Swedish asks names with the verb 'heta' (to be called): 'heter du' is literally are you called.
In 'hur gammal är du', 'du' is the word for you at every level, from strangers to bosses; formal 'ni' has mostly vanished.
'Tar över' is a two-word verb (take over): the spoken stress falls on 'över', not on 'tar'.
'Frysa' (to freeze) forms its past by vowel change: present 'fryser', past 'frös', with no '-de' ending.
'Kommer att' plus a verb expresses the future: 'kommer det att regna', with 'det' in between, means it is going to rain.
A non-subject first element forces the verb second and the subject third: 'i princip är vi'. Same rule as German and Dutch.
'Dit' means to there for motion; 'där' means there for location. Movement takes 'dit'.
'Gärna' means gladly or willingly; English has no single word for it. Here 'lika gärna' means just as gladly.
'Flugit' is the form of 'flyga' (fly) used after 'har': 'har aldrig flugit' means have never flown.
Add '-ut' to a compass word for direction: 'öster' plus 'ut' gives 'österut' (eastward).
'Fler' means more for countable things like 'fler frågor'; use 'mer' for uncountable amounts.
'Ta reda på' is a fixed expression meaning to find out; the three words stay together: 'tar reda på'.
'Hoppas' (to hope) always keeps its '-s': the past is 'hoppades', never 'hoppade'.
Definite forms double up: 'den nya lägenheten' has 'den' in front and the '-en' ending on the noun, plus '-a' on the adjective.
'Spela roll' means to matter: 'spelar ingen roll' is doesn't matter, literally plays no role.
'Fem i halv tre' means five minutes before half past two, so 2:25: Swedish counts minutes toward the half hour.
After 'föreslog att' (suggested that), Swedish normally uses 'skulle': 'föreslog att vi skulle vänta'.
In 'bor det många människor', 'det' is a filler subject like English there; the real subject follows the verb.
For in with seasons Swedish uses 'på': 'på sommaren' (in summer), 'på vintern' (in winter).
In 'jag är ny här', 'ny' agrees with its noun: 'ny' with en-words, 'nytt' with ett-words, 'nya' in definite and plural forms.
Exclamations use 'vad' plus an adjective and noun: 'vad fint väder det är' means what lovely weather it is.
An '-s' ending can make a verb passive: 'slutfördes' means was completed, with no extra word for was.
A place phrase first pushes the verb to second position: 'i Sverige', then 'är', then the subject 'sommaren'.
Ett-words like 'hus' add no plural ending: 'ett hus', 'två hus'; the definite plural is 'husen'.
'Man' is a generic subject meaning one, you, or people: 'ser man' means you can see.
Starting with 'aldrig' (never) adds emphasis and puts the verb before the subject: 'har jag sett'.
'Dålig' (bad) compares irregularly: 'dålig', 'värre', 'värst'; here 'värsta' means worst.
'Ju' pairs with 'desto' to mean the more ... the more: 'ju mer man övar', 'desto bättre blir man'.
